item.title: The Autonomous Era
item.description: We keep saying "autonomous" without saying what it means. Here is the definition I am working from, the three things standing in the way, and the reliability target that follows from taking it seriously.
item.content:encoded:
We’ve been talking about this for quite a while — we keep saying “autonomous, autonomous, autonomous” — but what do we mean by autonomous, and how does it even work?

The best thing that happened over the past three years was the launch of ClawdBot (OpenClaw). Not because it’s a nicer chatbot, or a more intelligent one, but because it worked autonomously — stitching over fifty tools, libraries, and platforms into one system. It made it feel magical.

The ClawdBot can go and read my Twitter, save my tone of voice into a simple markdown file, and schedule a post autonomously. It doesn’t stop there — it can do this all over again, every time, every day.

This is what we mean by autonomous: an agent that sits on the doctor’s EHR, keeps a pulse and checks every few hours for any changes, then autonomously takes the next best action, the next best decision, without any human interaction.

The hard truth

Before talking about how we have to move to building autonomous agents as fast as we can, I want to acknowledge the top three challenges in the company today:

  1. Integration speed and quality — blocking revenue growth.
  2. Audio capture stability — inherited tech debt in Copilot.
  3. Database and platform issues — the scalability ceiling in Firebase.

We’re making progress. But for the next 4–6 weeks, we’re taking this seriously. One hundred percent.

Revolution, meaning enterprise-ready

In order for us to move to the next phase, we’re going to hyper-focus for the next four to six weeks on integration, and on moving the platform from where it is to where it has to be.

That is a 500× reduction in tolerated failure.[1] This will be our highest priority in the company.

In the next 6–8 weeks, we need to push as hard as we can — not just to look like a larger enterprise company such as Athena or Cerner, $20 billion of technology that still breaks on clinicians every month, but to build a revolutionary platform that clinicians can rely on completely.

Yes, I mean it. One hundred percent uptime and stability.

Building an enterprise is very hard. Not because you need to get things right, but because you need multiple backups for everything — and on top of all that, you need the infrastructure to support it.

The autonomous position

“If you guys can do this for healthcare, this can truly disrupt the entire healthcare industry.”

— Chief of Staff, after watching our intelligence layer run

We’re extremely lucky to be in this position today as a healthcare AI player. We’re in the best position because we don’t have the huge number of customers that would make us too slow to move — and we’re not too small either. We have customers who will literally try anything we tell them.

This is the best time to build a $20 billion company: the ClawdBot for healthcare.

Our focus over the next few weeks will be on defining the core functions that all our agents perform, and on getting the team aligned on how agents safely collaborate and work autonomously for our customers.

It’s not going to be easy, but it’ll be hella fun.

  1. Called “quadruple nines” internally; strictly it’s six nines. The label matters less than the arithmetic: every additional nine is a ten-fold cut in the failure budget, and the last two are paid for in architecture, not effort. ↩︎

item.title: The Next Phase
item.description: We solved the hardest problem in our stack — hallucination — and now have to make it hold at enterprise grade. A status report on stability, capital, and the four weeks in front of us.
item.content:encoded:
Things are going to get hard from here. It’s not going to get easy.

However — we figured out one of the hardest problems in AI: getting these models to stop hallucinating. As a team, rolling this out and making sure it performs with enterprise-grade quality is one of the hardest things any company could ever do.

The bad news is we’re not there yet. The good news is we’re almost there.

We built this company from the ground up. It went $0 → $45M → $0 → $200M.

We want to make this company a $20 billion company by 2027.

This will not be easy. If it was easy, everybody would do it.

Where the focus goes

The entire focus of the company over the next couple of weeks:

  1. Get the platform stable.
  2. Invest energy and resources to fix it for good.
  3. Remove the integration bottleneck.

The leadership team is working day and night — hiring the right leaders, fixing the core fundamental problems, and getting the platform to where it needs to be.

It’s not going to be easy and we might lose some people along the way. But the journey to getting there will definitely be enjoyable. And when we get there, it’s going to pay off.

Platform stability

Where we were, and where we are. The bar plots the error rate rather than the stability figure, because at these magnitudes the interesting movement is in the residual, not the headline.[1]

Technical audio errors dropped from roughly 1,775 per week to 415 per week — a 4× reduction in four months.

AI generation stability

Generation errors fell from 13% to effectively zero. The model isn’t just better — it’s enterprise-ready.

Runway

We went out and secured capital from investors who don’t just write checks — they believe in what we’re building. LifeX. HP Ventures. Workday.

These aren’t passive investors. These are strategic partners who looked at our technology, our team, and our trajectory — and put real money behind it.

Runway went from six months to 1.1 years. That’s not just money — that’s time to execute. Time to get the platform right. Time to hire the right people. Time to win.

We’re not scrambling. We’re building — with the backing to see it through.

  1. A move from 95% to 99% looks like four points of improvement and is actually a five-fold reduction in failures. Always read the residual. ↩︎
